_readme: More seasons + facts for regular BD birds (non-overlapping with seasons_facts.json and overrides.json), drafted by an agent from the cited Wikipedia articles; plus name_sci display fixes (ids unchanged) confirmed from current English Wikipedia titles/taxoboxes. Name-fix-only entries carry just name_sci/_why/_sources. Needs human review.

facts: A big, slow-flying pigeon that spends long spells sitting still in the foliage of large fruiting trees.
Males have a whitish-grey cap; females have a browner cap and less gloss.
Outside the breeding season it may visit mangroves and small forested islands.
Northern populations migrate south to winter in India, while those nearer the tropics stay put.
It feeds mainly on seeds picked up from the ground.
Strays have turned up as far away as North America and Europe.
Named for the black half-collar, edged with white, on the back of its neck.
Its original range ran from Turkey through India; in the 20th century it spread right across Europe.
It has even reached Iceland as a vagrant.
A small, long-tailed dove of dry scrub and farmland that often becomes very tame around people.
In Asia it is often called the little brown dove.
Birds released from Perth Zoo in 1898 founded a wild population in Western Australia.
The male has a pinkish band across the upper breast above a broader orange one.
Feeding flocks move slowly and quietly through the trees, eating mainly small fruit.
Rival males fight by slapping each other with their wings.
Found from Nepal, northeast India and Bangladesh east to Vietnam.
Many authorities split it from the pompadour green pigeon complex.
A green pigeon of the eastern subcontinent and Southeast Asia, found across Bangladesh.
Besides lowland forest it also lives in mangroves.
Named for its long, pointed central tail feathers.
Resident in some parts of its range but nomadic in others, following fruiting trees.
Also called the kokla green pigeon.
Its range takes in Bangladesh, the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia.
A large forest pigeon, widespread as a resident from Nepal and India east to Indonesia and the Philippines.
The distinctive Sulawesi form is known as the chestnut-naped imperial pigeon.
Also called the maroon-backed or Hodgson's imperial pigeon.
It occurs in Bangladesh and across Southeast Asia, from mangroves at sea level up to 2,550 m in the Himalayas.
A nocturnal frogmouth related to the nightjars; both have bristles around the bill.
It is named after the British naturalist Brian Houghton Hodgson.
A very large nightjar with long ear-tufts, which it often keeps laid flat.
Unlike many nightjars it has no white on its wings or tail.
Its call at dawn and dusk is likened to a stone skipping on a frozen lake: clicks that get shorter and faster.
It is often seen on roads at night, its eyes glowing red in headlights.
It builds no nest, laying two marbled eggs on the bare ground.
A nocturnal bird with big eyes, a huge gape and superb camouflage.
In growing Asian cities, the flat roofs of tall buildings have become favourite nest sites.
Streaky brown camouflage makes it very hard to spot against soil and stones.
Mostly active after dark; its calls resemble those of curlews, hence the name stone-curlew.
Easily known by its long, upturned bill and bold black-and-white plumage.
It usually nests in colonies of 10 to 70 pairs on islets or dikes.
A large plover that breeds in the Arctic and is a long-distance migrant.
Outside the breeding season it is found on coasts almost worldwide.
Also called the peewit after its call.
Highly migratory, it winters as far south as northern India and Nepal.
In the breeding season the male performs a crazed, tumbling display flight.
A lapwing of rivers in northern and northeastern India and Southeast Asia that appears to be entirely sedentary.
It used to be called the spur-winged lapwing, a name now kept for an African species.
Russian breeders migrate south to winter in the Indian subcontinent, the Middle East and northeast Africa.
It is the only lapwing likely to be seen wading in anything but very shallow water.
Long yellow legs and a pure white tail make it distinctive.
A strongly migratory plover that breeds in Central Asian semi-deserts and winters on sandy beaches in South Asia, East Africa and Australasia.
In mixed flocks on Indian beaches it is told from the smaller sand plover by size and shape.
It was until recently placed in the genus Charadrius.
Some birds of the European race fly as far as India for the winter.
Alaskan birds fly non-stop across the Pacific to New Zealand: the longest known non-stop flight of any bird.
It probes coastal mudflats with its long, upturned bill for worms and shellfish.
Breeds in the far north and flies south to winter on coastlines almost worldwide, including South Asia.
It was once placed with the plovers but is now classed as a sandpiper.
One of the largest Calidris sandpipers; it breeds on Siberian tundra and winters on coasts from southern Asia to Australia.
It forms enormous flocks in winter.
It has one of the longest migrations of any bird; some American birds fly more than 9,000 miles from the Arctic to the tip of South America.
Some birds winter on the mudflats of the Gulf of Mannar and the east coast of India.
Away from the breeding grounds it feeds mostly on hard-shelled molluscs.
Its name comes from the Latin for 'a small sickle'.
It breeds in Arctic bogs and winters from East Africa through South Asia to Australasia, often flocking with dunlins.
It breeds only on the Siberian high Arctic tundra, arriving in June and leaving by August or September.
First-year birds stay in the wintering range all year rather than flying north to breed.
Habitat loss has made it Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.
Named after the Dutch naturalist Coenraad Jacob Temminck.
It winters at freshwater sites in tropical Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
In winter it looks like a tiny common sandpiper.
A tiny stint that breeds in Siberia and winters in South and Southeast Asia and Australasia.
Its name subminuta means 'nearly small', after its likeness to the little stint.
One of the most northerly breeding birds in the world, nesting only on the coldest Arctic tundra.
In the northern winter it is found on sea coasts almost worldwide, often in large flocks.
Migrating birds in the Delaware Bay eat large numbers of horseshoe crab eggs.
Its name is a dialect form of 'dunling', from dun, meaning dull brown.
Birds breeding in far northern Europe and Asia are long-distance migrants, wintering as far south as Africa and southern Asia.
A very small wader that breeds in the Arctic and winters south to Africa and South Asia.
In winter it forms flocks with other small waders on mudflats and the edges of pools.
The smallest snipe, and the only member of its genus.
It constantly bobs up and down as it feeds.
It winters as far as India and is silent in winter.
Its eyes are set so far back on its head that it can see all the way around, 360 degrees.
Asian populations migrate to the Indian subcontinent for the winter.
It probes the ground with its long, sensitive bill, so frozen ground makes it vulnerable.
A stocky snipe that breeds in the mountains of eastern Asia.
Some birds stay high in the mountains year-round, but others migrate to winter in places including northern India and Bangladesh.
A dark snipe that breeds in Himalayan alpine meadows above 3,000 m from May to July.
In winter it moves lower; it has been recorded as a vagrant in Bangladesh.
Breeds in northern Russia and spends the non-breeding season in southern Asia from Pakistan to Indonesia.
It is the most common migrant snipe in southern India, Sri Lanka and much of Southeast Asia.
Also called the forest snipe; it breeds in forest glades and meadows in Siberia and Mongolia.
The whole population migrates, wintering mainly in eastern and southern India, Southeast Asia and New Guinea.
Named after the British naturalist Robert Swinhoe, who described it in 1861.
Unlike most sandpipers it nests in trees.
It winters in the Indian subcontinent, among other places, and is very much a bird of freshwater.
It is not gregarious and usually feeds alone around the edges of ponds.
Black in breeding plumage but very pale in winter.
It breeds in the Arctic and migrates to tropical Asia, Africa and the Mediterranean for the winter.
Its name stagnatilis comes from the Latin for 'swamp'.
Most birds winter in Africa and India, usually alone or in small groups on freshwater wetlands.
In flight it shows a white wedge up its back.
Also called the grasshopper-bird or swallow-plover.
It breeds from northern Pakistan through South and East Asia and winters across the Indomalayan region and northern Australia.
A resident breeder in India, Bangladesh and Southeast Asia.
It nests from December to March on gravel or sand banks by rivers, laying 2–4 eggs in a ground scrape.
Northern breeders are strongly migratory, wintering south to southern Asia, Africa and the Americas.
In winter it loses its black cap, keeping only a dark patch through the eye.
Breeding adults have a black cap, orange-red legs and a narrow pointed bill.
Western Asian birds winter in the northern Indian Ocean.
First-summer birds usually stay in their wintering quarters instead of flying north.
Birds breeding on the Caspian Sea migrate to the Indian subcontinent, south to Sri Lanka.
Its black bill has a yellow tip, and it has a shaggy black crest.
Its name bengalensis means 'of Bengal', the place it was first described from.
It breeds on coasts from the Red Sea across the Indian Ocean to Australia.
A small bittern of freshwater marshes, mainly resident in the northern Indian subcontinent and East Asia.
It builds a small platform nest of reeds or twigs above water.
A dark bittern breeding in tropical Asia, including Bangladesh, east to China and Australia.
It is mainly resident, but some northern birds migrate short distances.
A medium-sized egret that is a resident breeder in southern and eastern Asia.
Some taxonomists put it in the genus Egretta or Mesophoyx instead of Ardea.
Also called the tiger bittern, it lives in forests, streams and marshes.
It has been found in Bangladesh and across South and East Asia.
It feeds mainly on the larvae of bees and wasps, which it tears from their combs.
Northern birds breed in Siberia and Japan and winter in Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent; elsewhere it is more or less resident.
Japanese birds fly non-stop over the East China Sea on migration.
A brown hawk with a thin, white-tipped black crest that it usually holds erect.
A resident of foothill forests from the eastern Himalayas to Bangladesh and Southeast Asia.
Named after the surgeon-naturalist Thomas C. Jerdon.
A small, crested raptor of dense forest that often perches on bare branches above the canopy.
Many populations migrate; in flight it looks rather like a crow and is often seen in small flocks.
A keystone scavenger that has been Critically Endangered since 2002 after a severe population crash.
It is not migratory but can travel hundreds of miles in a day searching for food.
Unlike the slender-billed vulture, it nests mainly on cliffs.
Critically Endangered: fewer than 870 mature birds were thought to remain in 2021.
It is found in north and central Bangladesh and nests in trees, unlike the cliff-nesting Indian vulture.
It is sedentary and does not migrate.
Native to Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Myanmar and Cambodia, in farmland and dry forest.
It was long treated as a race of the lesser spotted eagle and only recognised as a separate species in 2006.
A large migratory eagle that winters mainly in South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East and East Africa.
Birds wintering in India average about 5% bigger than those wintering in the Middle East.
It was once placed in the genus Aquila.
Northern populations migrate, spending November to February in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
On migration it uses almost any habitat except dense forest.
Almost the whole population migrates en masse each year, and in winter it reaches much of the Indian subcontinent.
In winter it feeds sluggishly, focusing on insect swarms and landfills.
It was once lumped with the tawny eagle.
A hawk with a striking white iris, a rufous tail and a white throat with a dark central stripe.
A resident in Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Myanmar and across India's plains.
It sits upright on perches for long periods; pairs call a lot as they soar together in the breeding season.
Breeds in northeast China, Mongolia and southeast Siberia and winters in places including northeast India and Bangladesh.
It was previously lumped with the western marsh harrier.
Breeds on the steppes of eastern Europe and Central Asia and winters mainly in India and Southeast Asia.
A pair nested in a Dutch barley field in 2017, the first known breeding in the Netherlands.
Named for the male's distinctive black-and-white plumage.
It breeds from Lake Baikal to North Korea and winters from eastern India through Southeast Asia, hunting over paddy fields and swamps.
A crested hawk of tropical Asian lowlands that stays put all year.
It was formerly placed in the genus Accipiter and is now Lophospiza trivirgata.
Its name 'besra' comes from the Hindi word for this bird.
A resident of dense forest across southern Asia; it builds a new nest every year.
In winter it ventures into more open woodland and cultivation.
A fish eagle seen most often along hill streams and fast-flowing water.
Its range takes in Bangladesh, Nepal and Southeast Asia.
In northern India it breeds from March to August.
haliaeetus-humilis._why: English Wikipedia lead and taxobox (genus = Icthyophaga) use Icthyophaga humilis.

facts: It lives in tall grassland and swamps, roosting in flattened 'tunnels' through the vegetation.
It feeds mainly on small rodents.
An altitudinal migrant of hill forests from Pakistan and the Himalayas to Malaysia.
Its call is a short, high, two-note whistle, 'plew-plew'.
A small scops owl found from eastern Arabia through the Indian subcontinent.
It is very similar to the slightly larger collared scops owl.
A scops owl with a very wide range across South, Southeast and East Asia.
It nests in tree holes, especially in mahua trees, from February to April.
A big horned owl of rocky, scrubby hills in the Indian subcontinent, usually seen in pairs.
Its deep, booming call carries at dawn and dusk.
It was once treated as a race of the Eurasian eagle-owl.
Also called the forest eagle-owl, a formidable-looking owl of old forests in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
It is now placed in the genus Ketupa.
Found from Pakistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh east to China.
It lives in forests, wooded wetlands and even roadside avenues of big old trees.
Its scientific name comes from the Coromandel Coast, where the first specimen was collected.
A fish owl of forest tracts with mountain streams, from southern Nepal to Bangladesh, China and Vietnam.
In India it breeds from November to February.
The smallest owl in Asia, just 15 cm long and about 60 g.
A resident of hill and mountain forests from the Himalayas to eastern China and Malaysia.
Also called the cuckoo owlet; one of the larger pygmy owls.
Mostly insectivorous, it also takes lizards, small rodents and birds.
The race rufescens lives in northeast India, Bangladesh and north Myanmar.
A small owlet of the Indian subcontinent, usually found by its calls at dawn and dusk.
It nests in tree hollows, breeding from March to May in India.
An earless owl found in India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and east to China and Indonesia.
It is uniformly dark brown above with a brown or rufous facial disc.
Also known as the brown hawk-owl; a resident breeder in India, Bangladesh and across tropical South Asia.
It is common even in towns and cities like Colombo.
A stray was photographed on St. Paul Island, Alaska, in 2007.
A kingfisher of shaded forest streams, darker than the common kingfisher and lacking its rufous ear stripe.
Males have an all-dark bill; females have a reddish lower mandible.
It ranges from India across Bangladesh to Malaysia and is largely resident.
A pocket-sized forest kingfisher, also called the three-toed kingfisher.
Its breeding range includes eastern Bangladesh; some birds migrate south to the Malay Peninsula in winter.
Linnaeus described it from 'the small kingfisher from Bengall'.
A resident barbet of hill forests; the race cyanotis lives from southeastern Nepal and Bangladesh to southern China.
It nests in tree cavities.
A large barbet of forests up to 3,000 m.
A resident of the Himalayas and hills of Bangladesh and Southeast Asia.
A fruit-eating barbet of the Terai and the Brahmaputra basin to Southeast Asia.
It nests in holes in tree trunks.
A member of the woodpecker family whose bill is shorter and less dagger-like than other woodpeckers'.
Most populations migrate, wintering in tropical Africa and in southern Asia from Iran to the Indian subcontinent.
A tiny woodpecker found across the subcontinent and Southeast Asia, including Bangladesh.
It often forages in bamboo jungle.
A tiny woodpecker of dense forest with vines and bamboo, from northern India and Bangladesh to Vietnam.
It is fairly common, with no particular known threats.
A small, dark pied woodpecker with dark eyes; males have a red nape.
Its range extends from the Himalayas and Manchuria to Southeast Asia.
A pied woodpecker found in Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, India and Myanmar.
The freckle-breasted woodpecker of Southeast Asia used to be lumped with it.
It drills rows of small pits in tree bark, which is why it was once grouped with the sapsuckers.
Generally uncommon; it has vanished from parts of its range as deciduous forest has been cleared.
A woodpecker of densely wooded ravines in evergreen and mixed forest, from 50 m up to 2,750 m.
Bangladesh is among the countries where it is most commonly found.
Also called the greater goldenback; it is widespread from the northern subcontinent to Borneo and Java.
A brown woodpecker that feeds mainly on ants and termites.
It builds its nest inside the carton nests of tree ants.
It breeds in the dry pre-monsoon period from February to June.
A bamboo specialist found in Bangladesh, northeast India and Southeast Asia.
A 2017 DNA study found it actually sits inside the flameback genus Dinopium.
Also called the Himalayan goldenback; very little is known about it.
A year-round resident of mature sal and semi-evergreen forests in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar and Nepal.
A three-toed woodpecker of South and Southeast Asia.
Shy and secretive, it lives in open forest, scrub and mangroves but avoids towns.
A widespread and often common woodpecker from India and Bangladesh east to Indonesia.
Found from far southeastern Bangladesh to the central Malay Peninsula, in lowland forest and mangroves.
The only Bangladesh specimen of the laced woodpecker turned out to be one of these.
Its range runs from Europe across Asia to the Pacific and south to the Himalaya and Malay Peninsula.
In late autumn it adds berries and other fruit to its diet.
A big woodpecker with a yellow crest, found from northern and eastern India to southeastern China and Sumatra.
Probably the largest woodpecker still alive, since the imperial and ivory-billed woodpeckers are likely extinct.
It lives in Bangladesh and across the subcontinent and Southeast Asia, in semi-open forest with tall trees.
Young birds probably stay with their parents until the next breeding season.
A tiny falcon only 18 cm long; when perched it looks rather like a shrike.
It flies with rapid wingbeats broken by long glides.
It was first described from a specimen collected in Bengal.
Its genus contains the smallest birds of prey in the world.
It nests in old woodpecker holes and stays in the same area all year.
A falcon with a chestnut-red cap, found in open plains of the Indian subcontinent and in Africa.
It was described from a specimen obtained at Chandernagore in Bengal, where locals called it 'chicquera'.
It breeds in southeastern Siberia and northern China and migrates in big flocks across India and the Arabian Sea to winter in southern Africa.
Birds crossing India are thought to ride strong westward winds at about 3,000 m.
A small, slim falcon; the nominate race winters in Africa and South Asia.
A smaller race is resident from Myanmar to south China.
Found across the Indian subcontinent, including Bangladesh.
Once one of the region's commonest falcons, it has declined because of pesticides and its use as a decoy to trap larger falcons.
Famous for its speed; its English and scientific names mean 'wandering falcon'.
The northern race calidus is completely migratory and winters as far south as South Asia.
The South Asian race peregrinator is known as the shaheen falcon.
A tailorbird of lowland forest and mangroves in Bangladesh, northeast India and Southeast Asia.
It is often kept as a pet.
The nominate race lives in east and northeast India, Bhutan, Bangladesh, south China and Myanmar.
Easily told by a smoky-grey band across the breast that contrasts with its white throat.
It loses the breast band outside the breeding season.
The nominate race is resident from the Gangetic plains east to Bangladesh.
A resident breeder in Bangladesh, India and Sri Lanka, in dry grassland, scrub and sometimes gardens.
The sexes look alike, but in the breeding season the male has a blacker bill and mouth.
A prinia of the southern Himalayan foothills, the northeastern subcontinent and Southeast Asia.
A common resident of gardens and farmland across the subcontinent, including Bangladesh.
Its small size, upright tail and ashy-grey colours make it easy to identify.
Known as the 'finest tailor of all birds', it stitches its nest from plants and spider silk.
In the breeding season the male turns golden and grows a much shorter tail.
A big warbler, nearly as large as the great reed warbler, that breeds from south Siberia to Mongolia.
It winters in tropical South and Southeast Asia, in reeds, bushes and thick undergrowth.
Breeds from central Russia to western China and winters in the Indian subcontinent as far south as Sri Lanka.
It has spread west in recent decades and now nests as far as Finland.
A small reed warbler that breeds in the central Palearctic and winters in Bangladesh, India and Pakistan.
Its name agricola is Latin for 'farmer'.
It breeds from Afghanistan to China and winters in Myanmar, Thailand and Bangladesh.
It was first described by Robert Swinhoe in 1870.
It breeds from the Baltic almost to Lake Baikal and winters in India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
It has been spreading west and first bred in Scotland in 2024.
In winter it lives in trees in both wet and dry places, not just reeds.
Once lumped with the great reed warbler, it breeds in East Asia and winters from northeast India through Southeast Asia.
Outside reedbeds it also turns up in paddy fields, grassland and scrub.
Noisy and conspicuous, it often sings from exposed perches on grass tops, bushes and telephone wires.
It is now the only species in its genus, Megalurus.
Also called the rusty-rumped warbler; it breeds in the eastern Palearctic and winters from India east to Indonesia.
A skulker of tall grass near water; as a vagrant it turns up with some regularity on Fair Isle, Shetland.
Endemic to the Indian subcontinent, it skulks in tall, dense grassland, often in marshes.
It was once described as common in parts of Bangladesh, but grassland loss threatens it.
Long thought to be sedentary, it may in fact migrate within the subcontinent.
A forest bulbul; the race atriceps ranges from northeastern India and Bangladesh to the Greater Sundas.
It is now placed in the genus Microtarsus.
A bulbul of forest and dense scrub from the Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia.
Its name comes from 'flavescent', a yellowish colour.
The nominate race lives in northeastern India, northeastern Bangladesh and western Myanmar, in hill forest.
A local endemic of northeastern India and the Sylhet and Chittagong divisions of Bangladesh.
It was split from the olive bulbul in 2017, after DNA showed the two diverged 1.7 million years ago.
A hill-forest bulbul whose range includes northeastern Bangladesh.
It often moves down to the lowlands in winter, though rarely right down to sea level.
A bulbul of broadleaf evergreen forest between about 800 and 2,600 m.
Named after the East India Company surgeon John McClelland.
A bulbul of moist lowland forest from the eastern Himalayas to Myanmar and western Thailand.
A tiny leaf warbler that breeds in the east Palearctic and winters mainly in tropical South and Southeast Asia, including Bangladesh.
It is abundant, and small numbers now also winter in western Europe.
It breeds in southern Siberia and winters in Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.
Its scientific name honours the German astronomer Ludwig Schwarz.
Breeds from eastern Siberia to Japan and winters from eastern India and Bangladesh to Java.
It often joins mixed flocks of small birds.
A strongly migratory leaf warbler that breeds across Asia and winters in India.
A few pairs nest each year as far west as Germany.
Named for its simple 'chiff-chaff' song.
It winters in southern Asia, southern Europe and north Africa, and is among the first songbirds back in spring.
A tiny, almost tailless bush warbler of moist hill forest, from the Himalayas through southern China and Indochina.
A small warbler of forest, found from Bangladesh and the Himalayas through Southeast Asia to Indonesia.
A small warbler of moist lowland forest, found in Bangladesh and from the Himalayas to Taiwan.
Despite its name it is not a true tailorbird; it is now placed in the bush warbler family Cettiidae.
It lives in hill forest of the Purvanchal range, southern China and Southeast Asia.
A skulking bush warbler of the Himalayas, south China and Southeast Asia.
A babbler of grassy and thorny scrub and farmland, found from Pakistan through India to Bangladesh and China.
Usually seen in small groups of five to fifteen, especially outside the breeding season.
Despite its name it is more closely related to the parrotbills than to true babblers.
A parrotbill of moist hill forest from the Himalayas to Indochina and Hainan.
A parrotbill of moist forest from the eastern Himalayas to Indochina.
A thick-billed parrotbill found in Bangladesh, India and east to China and Vietnam.
A small, round, short-tailed parrotbill of bamboo and evergreen forest with tall grass.
It moves lower down the hills at certain times of year to escape the cold.
The only species in its genus; the race bengalensis lives in the lower Himalayas, Bangladesh and northeastern India.
Its range has recently been found to extend further west, into southern Uttarakhand.
Also called the yellow-breasted babbler; widespread from Nepal and Bangladesh through Southeast Asia.
It breeds from February to July and builds a loose ball-shaped nest of grass and leaves.
A small babbler that forages in little groups in low scrub and tall grass.
Like most babblers it does not migrate and has short, rounded wings and a weak flight.
A small babbler with yellow underparts and a golden-yellow, finely striped crown.
It lives in forests from the eastern Himalayan foothills to Southeast Asia.
The buff-chested babbler is now usually merged into the rufous-fronted babbler.
That species ranges from the eastern Himalayan foothills to Sumatra and Borneo.
It has the long, down-curved reddish-orange bill typical of scimitar babblers and a long white eyebrow.
It lives in forest from northeast India to Southeast Asia, often in bamboo.
Its slender, strongly curved bill once earned it a genus of its own, Xiphirhynchus.
It lives in moist hill forest from the Himalayas to northwestern Vietnam.
A scimitar babbler of hill forest found in Bangladesh, the Himalayas and east to Vietnam.
It forms mixed flocks with other species.
A scimitar babbler of moist forest in Bangladesh, the Himalayas and Southeast Asia.
A big scimitar babbler of moist forest in Bangladesh and across Southeast Asia.
A scimitar babbler of the Himalayas from northeast Pakistan to Bhutan and Myanmar.
It was formerly lumped with the red-eyed scimitar babbler of Myanmar and Thailand.
A small forest babbler found from the Himalayas and Bangladesh to Indonesia; twelve subspecies are recognised.
A babbler of moist forest from the eastern Himalayas to central Myanmar and southwestern China.
Its name is misleading: it is not closely related to the 'typical' fulvettas.
It lives in hill forest from the Himalayas to north-central Vietnam.
A small, noisy fulvetta with a streaked chestnut crown and bright rufous wing feathers against black coverts.
Its name is misleading, as it is not a close relative of the typical fulvettas.
A fulvetta of moist lowland forest from the Himalayas through Indochina to southwestern Cambodia.
A grass babbler of the Brahmaputra plains of Assam and nearby northern Bangladesh.
It prefers tall grassland near large rivers or swamps and is easiest to find when singing in the breeding season.
Also called the spotted babbler; it forages in small groups on the forest floor, flipping over leaf litter.
Hard to see but easy to hear, with loud calls and a distinctive morning song.
Endemic to the Brahmaputra floodplain and nearby hills of northeast India and eastern Bangladesh.
A babbler found mainly in eastern Bangladesh, Bhutan, northeast India, Yunnan, Myanmar and Vietnam.
A babbler of moist forest found in Bangladesh and across Southeast Asia.
A wren-babbler of hill forest from northeastern India to southern China.
A stout, short-tailed babbler that forages in pairs in dense undergrowth near the ground.
It is resident in east and south Bangladesh, including around Jessore and Khulna.
Also called the rufous-rumped grassbird; it lives in tall vegetation by swamps and rivers in the lowlands of Bangladesh, northern India, Bhutan and Nepal.
It is threatened by habitat loss.
Formerly called the quaker babbler in India.
It forages in trees, sometimes hanging tit-like from branches, and also visits flowers for nectar.
The race fusca lives in eastern Bangladesh.
An omnivorous babbler found in southern Asia from Pakistan to Myanmar.
A 2018 DNA study moved it from Turdoides to the revived genus Argya.
A babbler of seasonally flooded lowland grassland in Bangladesh, Nepal and northeast India.
It is threatened by the loss of its grassland habitat.
A highly social, noisy laughingthrush of forest and scrub from the Himalayan foothills to Southeast Asia.
The race patkaicus lives in northeast India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
It has one of the widest ranges of any laughingthrush.
A laughingthrush of moist forest across the eastern Himalayas, southern China and Indochina.
A laughingthrush of the northern subcontinent; the race assamensis lives in southeast Assam, east Bangladesh and west Myanmar.
A laughingthrush of moist forest found in Bangladesh and from the Himalayas to Vietnam.
It has been introduced to Hawaii.
A laughingthrush of moist forest in Bangladesh, the Himalayas, China and Myanmar.
It is non-migratory and spends its whole life in the same area.
A laughingthrush of moist forest found in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam.
The only species in its genus, living in moist hill forest of the subcontinent and Southeast Asia, including Bangladesh.
A bird of hill forest found in Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, northeast India, Nepal and western Yunnan.
It moves through dense undergrowth in pairs or in flocks, sometimes with other species.
Also called the blue-winged siva; it has been placed in the genera Minla and Siva in the past.
It lives in moist hill forest from Bangladesh and the Himalayas to Malaysia.
Its name dauurica refers to Dauria, a region of southeastern Siberia.
It breeds in Japan, eastern Siberia and the Himalayas and winters in tropical southern Asia.
A first-winter bird at Flamborough Head, England, in 2007 drew hundreds of birdwatchers.
It often runs along the ground with its long tail cocked, showing chestnut under the tail.
Males can be so aggressive in the breeding season that they attack their own reflections.
It often lives close to people and perches on rooftops.
A famous songster native to dense scrub and secondary forest of South and Southeast Asia.
Its popularity as a cage bird has led to escaped populations, including in Hawaii and Taiwan, where it is invasive.
A dull bluish-grey flycatcher with a rufous chest; males lack the bright blue of most Cyornis species.
